claims.statement: At thirteen he served Xianzu and as a clansman was loved no differently than a son

translationRepairs: While Wuhuang held Yanmen, thirteen-year-old Siyuan, then in Dai, impressed Xianzu with his riding and archery; Xianzu stroked him and said, "Spirit like your father—you may wait on me."
While Wuhuang held Yanmen, Xiaocheng passed away; the Emperor was just thirteen and skilled at mounted archery; Xianzu saw him, stroked him, and said, "Spirit like your father—you may wait on me."
孝成厭代 is a death euphemism for Xiaocheng, not a location; the original invents that Siyuan was then in Dai.

When Wuhuang held Yanmen, Xiaocheng was in Dai, and the Emperor was just thirteen, skilled at mounted archery; Xianzu saw him, stroked him, and said, "Spirit like your father—you may attend at my side."

When Wuhuang held Yanmen, Xiaocheng passed away, and the Emperor was just thirteen, skilled at mounted archery; Xianzu saw him, stroked him, and said, "Spirit like your father—you may attend at my side."
厭代 marks Xiaocheng's death, so 'was in Dai' is a toponym error.
In Qianning 3 Liang armies pressed Yan and Yun; Zhu Xuan of Yan begged Wuhuang for aid.
In Qianning 3 Liang armies pressed Yan and Yun; Zhu Xuan of Yun begged Wuhuang for aid.
鄆帥朱瑄 is the commander of Yun; Yan (兗) is a besieged prefecture, not his title.
In the third year of Qianning, Liang forces pressed Yan and Yun fiercely; Yan military commissioner Zhu Xuan begged Wuhuang for rescue.
In the third year of Qianning, Liang forces pressed Yan and Yun fiercely; Yun military commissioner Zhu Xuan begged Wuhuang for rescue.
鄆帥 is Yun's military commissioner, not Yan's.
His great-great-grandmother, Lady Cui of the State of Wei, was posthumously given the temple name Empress Xiaogong Zhao.
His great-great-grandmother, Lady Cui of the State of Wei, was posthumously given the posthumous title Empress Xiaogong Zhao.
追諡 is a posthumous title; the adjacent sentence reserves 廟號 for Huizu, so 'temple name' is wrong.
Cornered, Xingqin bound his face and surrendered; Siyuan gave him wine, clapped his back, and said, "My boy, what a fighter!"
Cornered, Xingqin bound his hands behind his back and surrendered; Siyuan gave him wine, clapped his back, and said, "My boy, what a fighter!"
面縛 is the surrender posture of hands bound behind the back, not binding the face.
Xingqin was cornered, bound his face, and begged surrender; the Emperor poured wine for him to drink, patted his back, and said, "My boy, what a brave fellow!"
Xingqin was cornered, bound his hands behind his back, and begged surrender; the Emperor poured wine for him to drink, patted his back, and said, "My boy, what a brave fellow!"
面縛 names the bound-hands surrender rite, not a literal binding of the face.
In the fourth month Xiangzhou's Zhang Yun fled; he was then made Xiang prefectural governor.
In the fourth month Xiangzhou's Zhang Yun fled; the Emperor was then made Xiang prefectural governor.
乃以帝為相州刺史 appoints the Emperor after Zhang Yun fled; the pronoun 'he' wrongly gives the office to Zhang Yun.

In the fourth month of year 14 Khitan Anbajian besieged Youzhou; Zhou Dewei sent urgent word, and Zhuangzong asked his generals how to relieve it; they said the Khitan could not stay long and should be struck only after they withdrew for hunger."

In the fourth month of year 14 Khitan Anbajian besieged Youzhou; Zhou Dewei sent urgent word, and Zhuangzong asked his generals how to relieve it; they said the Khitan could not stay long and should be struck only after they withdrew for hunger.
The idiomatic sentence paraphrases 諸將咸言 and should not end with a stray closing quotation mark.

The Emperor said to the generals, "Enemy horse live on the saddle and need no camps; moreover they are many and we few—we should hold arrows in the mouth, clamp the horses' mouths, steal along streams and ravines, and strike them unprepared."

The Emperor said to the generals, "Enemy horse live on the saddle and need no camps; moreover they are many and we few—we should hold gags in the mouth, clamp the horses' mouths, steal along streams and ravines, and strike them unprepared."
銜枚 is soldiers holding wooden gags for a silent march, not arrows in the mouth.

That day the generals congratulated him; Cunxu handed wine to Siyuan and said, "Yesterday at Chaocheng many of you wanted to abandon Yan and make the river the border; only the deputy overall commander held the front and Chongtao schemed within—had I listened to Li Shaohong and his crowd, the cause would be dust."

That day the generals congratulated him; Cunxu handed wine to Siyuan and said, "Yesterday at Chaocheng many of you wanted to abandon Yun and make the river the border; only the deputy overall commander held the front and Chongtao schemed within—had I listened to Li Shaohong and his crowd, the cause would be dust."
棄鄆州 is Yun, the prefecture Zhuangzong had just entered; Yan is a later, different toponym.

That day the generals offered congratulations; Zhuangzong passed wine to the Emperor, saying, "Yesterday I was at Chaocheng; many of you urged me to abandon Yanzhou and take the river as boundary; relying on the deputy overall commander to repel insult in front and Chongtao to scheme within, if I had believed Li Shaohong and his sort, the great affair would already have been swept away."

That day the generals offered congratulations; Zhuangzong passed wine to the Emperor, saying, "Yesterday I was at Chaocheng; many of you urged me to abandon Yunzhou and take the river as boundary; relying on the deputy overall commander to repel insult in front and Chongtao to scheme within, if I had believed Li Shaohong and his sort, the great affair would already have been swept away."
鄆州 is Yunzhou; Yanzhou would be 兗州, which this sentence does not use.
In the sixth month he became Grand Preceptor, took Bian as military commissioner, and replaced Li Cun'an as Han and non-Han overall commander.
In the sixth month he became Grand Commandant, took Bian as military commissioner, and replaced Li Cunshen as Han and non-Han overall commander.
進位太尉 is Grand Commandant, and 李存審 is Li Cunshen, not Grand Preceptor or Li Cun'an.
Sixth month: he was promoted to Grand Preceptor, transferred to hold Bianzhou, replacing Li Cun'an as Han and non-Han overall commander.
Sixth month: he was promoted to Grand Commandant, transferred to hold Bianzhou, replacing Li Cunshen as Han and non-Han overall commander.
The source has 太尉 and 李存審; Grand Preceptor and Li Cun'an are mistranslations.
On the sixth day of the second month in the fourth year Zhao Zaili rebelled at Ye; Cunxu sent Yuan Xingqin against him;
On the sixth day of the second month in the fourth year Zhao Zaili rebelled at Weizhou; Cunxu sent Yuan Xingqin against him;
據魏州反 is Weizhou; Ye (鄴) is not named in this sentence.
Fourth year, second month, sixth day: Zhao Zaili held Ye prefecture in revolt; Zhuangzong sent Yuan Xingqin to lead troops against him;
Fourth year, second month, sixth day: Zhao Zaili held Weizhou in revolt; Zhuangzong sent Yuan Xingqin to lead troops against him;
魏州 is Weizhou, not Ye prefecture.
Xingqin was unfavorable and withdrew to guard Weizhou.
Xingqin was unsuccessful and withdrew to guard Weizhou.
不利 means the campaign went badly, so 'was unfavorable' is wrong; 'met with reverse' is still awkward.
Siyuan shouted and rebuked their treason; they answered, "Yesterday at Beizhou garrison you showed no mercy;
Siyuan shouted and rebuked their treason; they answered, "Yesterday at the Beizhou garrison the sovereign showed no generous pardon;
主上 is the reigning sovereign, not the 令公 they are addressing; 'you showed no mercy' misattributes the pardon.
We have agreed with the garrison to drive off the other columns; we want you emperor south of the river and our lord emperor north."
We have agreed with the garrison to drive off the other columns; we want the sovereign emperor south of the river and you, our lord, emperor north."
欲主上帝河南，請令公帝河北 assigns the south to the sovereign and Siyuan to the north; the original swaps the two.
Siyuan wept and refused; they shouted, "If you will not go north, where will you go?
Siyuan wept and refused; they shouted, "Where does our lord mean to go?
令公欲何之 asks where he means to go; the original invents a refused journey north.
Xingqin held Weizhou and slandered him by memorial; Siyuan answered; Cunxu sent his son Congshen and the eunuch Bai Congxun with an edict.
Xingqin held Weizhou and slandered him by memorial; Siyuan answered; Cunxu sent Siyuan's son Congshen and the eunuch Bai Congxun with an edict.
帝子從審 is the annals' 帝 (Siyuan), not Zhuangzong's son; 'the Emperor's son' after Cunxu remains ambiguous, so name Siyuan.
At dawn Zhu Shouyin sent word, "Luoyang is burning and looting will not stop—come quickly."
At dawn Zhu Shouyin sent word, "The capital is in great disorder; burning and looting will not stop—come quickly."
The report names 京城 and 京師, not Luoyang; the next sentence's arrival at Luoyang does not license inventing the city in this quote.
Jiji's Shu campaign had not returned; Siyuan told Zhu Shouyin, "Patrol well and await the Prince of Wei.
At that time Prince of Wei Jiji's campaign against Shu had not yet returned; the Emperor told Zhu Shouyin, "Kindly patrol and soothe, and await the Prince of Wei."
時魏王繼岌征蜀未還 is omitted in part, 公善巡撫 is a courteous imperative to patrol and soothe, and the original speech lacks its closing quote.

(The 《Miscellaneous Dreams of the Northern Realm》 records: Zhuangzong's younger brothers Cunji and Cunque hid in a south-mountain peasant household; someone reported this to An Chonghui, and Chonghui said, "The lord below has issued an edict to seek them; the Emperor's benevolence will surely not harm them—better secretly order them killed."

(The 《Miscellaneous Dreams of the Northern Realm》 records: Zhuangzong's younger brothers Cunji and Cunque hid in a south-mountain peasant household; someone reported this to An Chonghui, and Chonghui said, "The ruler has issued an edict to seek them; the Emperor's benevolence will surely not harm them—better secretly order them killed."
主上以下詔 is 主上 plus 下詔, 'the ruler has issued an edict,' not a lord who is below.
He thus made the living smear themselves with ashes and soldiers hunger in cold, making a sore upon All-under-Heaven and exhausting human weariness to the limit.
He thus drove the living into utter misery and soldiers into hunger and cold, making a sore upon All-under-Heaven and exhausting human weariness to the limit.
生靈塗炭 is the idiom of the people plunged into misery, not a literal smearing with ashes.
Summer and autumn field taxes may add nothing beyond the original grain levy per dou and ground-head money.
Summer and autumn field taxes may add nothing beyond the original grain levy in shi and dou and ground-head money.
The levy is 石斗, the paired grain measures shi and dou; the chapter's 石鬥 is the 鬥/斗 variant, not a tax counted only per dou.
Summer and autumn field taxes, apart from the originally levied grain per dou and the ground-head money, may have no further surcharges.
Summer and autumn field taxes, apart from the originally levied grain in shi and dou and the ground-head money, may have no further surcharges.
CText reads 石斗 for the original grain measures; 'per dou' drops 石 and treats the 鬥 variant as a single unit.
